questions.prompt:
A length is measured as (2.40 ± 0.05) m.
(a) Calculate the percentage uncertainty. (2)
(b) The length is squared to obtain an area proportional to $L^2$. Estimate the percentage uncertainty in the area. (2)
(c) Explain the difference between a random and a systematic error. (3)
hints: For powers, multiply fractional uncertainty by the power.
questions.solution:
(a) Percentage uncertainty $=0.05/2.40\times100=2.08\%$. [M1 A1]
(b) For $L^2$, percentage uncertainty $\approx2\times2.08=4.17\%$. [M1 A1]
(c) Random errors vary unpredictably between readings and can be reduced by repeats; systematic errors shift readings consistently and are not removed by averaging. [B1 B1 B1]

questions.prompt:
(i) Name the error avoided by closing a micrometer's jaws before use. (1)
(ii) Explain why recording 45.043 mm as 45.0 mm cannot be justified. (1)
(iii) Describe how to measure a tube's external diameter accurately. (2)
questions.solution:
(i) Zero error [B1]
(ii) Discards precision the instrument provides [B1]
(iii) Measure at several points and orientations along the tube [B1]
Use the ratchet; calculate the mean [B1]

questions.prompt: A student measured a slide's mass on a balance with 0.01 g resolution and repeated it, claiming precise, accurate results. Comment. (4)
questions.solution:
Resolution relates to precision, not accuracy [B1]
Repeats reduce random error only [B1]
Systematic errors (e.g. zero error) aren't removed by repeating [B1]
Balance should be calibrated / zeroed to ensure accuracy [B1]

questions.prompt: Angular velocities of 0.125, 0.112, 0.118, 0.123 and 0.116 rad s⁻¹ were measured. Calculate the mean and its percentage uncertainty. (3)
questions.solution:
Mean = 0.119 rad s⁻¹ [M1]
Half range = 0.0065 [M1]
5.5% [A1]

questions.prompt: Using a = ω²r with ω uncertain by 5.5% and r by 1.0%, calculate the percentage uncertainty in a. (2)
Classify displacement, energy, momentum and power as scalar or vector. (2)
questions.solution:
Vectors: displacement, momentum [B1]
Scalars: energy, power [B1]

questions.prompt:
(i) Distinguish accuracy and precision. (2)
(ii) Explain how a thermometer reading can be precise but not accurate. (2)
questions.solution:
(i) Accuracy: closeness to the true value [B1]
Precision: closeness of repeated readings [B1]
(ii) Repeated readings agree closely [B1]
But a systematic error (e.g. not calibrated) shifts them from the true value [B1]

questions.prompt: A balance has resolution 0.2 g and each disc has mass 4.0 g. Calculate the minimum number of discs for a mass uncertainty below 0.5%. (3)
questions.solution:
Need total mass > 0.2 ÷ 0.005 = 40 g [M1]
40 ÷ 4.0 = 10 [M1]
At least 11 discs [A1]

questions.prompt: Washer diameters are 4.52 ± 0.02 cm and 2.53 ± 0.02 cm. Show the percentage uncertainty in the ring area is about 3%. (4)
questions.solution:
d₁² = 20.4 ± 0.18 cm²; d₂² = 6.40 ± 0.10 cm² [M1]
Difference = 14.0 ± 0.28 cm² [M1]
% = 0.28 ÷ 14.0 × 100 [M1]
= 2% – about 3% with rounding [A1]

questions.prompt: A student says measuring 43.5 cm with a metre rule to 0.1 cm means high accuracy. Comment. (3)
questions.solution:
0.1 cm is resolution, not accuracy [B1]
Reading both ends gives larger uncertainty [B1]
Systematic errors such as a worn rule end aren't reduced [B1]

questions.prompt: Pendulum lengths of 85.5, 86.0, 87.5 and 85.5 cm are recorded. Calculate a suitable mean. (2)
questions.solution:
87.5 cm is anomalous [B1]
Mean = 85.7 cm [B1]

questions.prompt: A charged sphere hangs at an angle in a horizontal field. Name the three forces acting and describe how they form a closed triangle. (2)
questions.solution:
Weight, tension and horizontal electric force [B1]
In equilibrium they form a closed vector triangle [B1]

questions.prompt:
(i) Distinguish error and uncertainty. (2)
(ii) Give two reasons a measurement may be uncertain. (2)
questions.solution:
(i) Error: difference between a measured and true value [B1]
Uncertainty: range within which the true value is likely to lie [B1]
(ii) Instrument resolution [B1]
Random variation in readings / human reaction time [B1]

questions.prompt: What do electron deflection and electron diffraction experiments show? (2)
questions.solution:
Deflection (specific charge): electrons are charged particles [B1]
Diffraction: electrons also behave as waves [B1]

questions.prompt: A balance reads to 0.01 g. Comment on the claim that this makes force values accurate and precise. (2)
questions.solution:
Small resolution improves precision, not accuracy [B1]
Systematic errors (zero error, calibration) may remain [B1]

questions.prompt:
A body of mass 2.0 kg is pulled horizontally by a force of 12 N. A resistive force of 3 N acts in the opposite direction.
(a) Calculate the acceleration. (3)
(b) Starting from rest, calculate the speed after 4.0 s assuming constant acceleration. (2)
(c) Explain one limitation of the constant-resistance model. (2)
questions.solution:
(a) Resultant force $=12-3=9$ N. $a=F/m=4.50$ m s$^{-2}$. [M1 M1 A1]
(b) $v=u+at=0+4.50\times4=18.00$ m s$^{-1}$. [M1 A1]
(c) Real drag generally changes with speed/environment, so it is unlikely to remain constant. [B1 B1]

questions.prompt: A 70 kg go-kart travels up a 6.0° slope at a constant 3.0 m s⁻¹ against a resistive force of 20 N. Calculate the useful power output. (4)
questions.solution:
Weight component = 70 × 9.81 × sin 6.0° = 71.8 N [M1]
Driving force = 71.8 + 20 = 91.8 N [M1]
P = 91.8 × 3.0 [M1]
= 275 W [A1]

questions.prompt: A cyclist moves at constant velocity on level ground. Name the four forces acting on the bicycle and cyclist and state how they are related. (3)
questions.solution:
Weight and normal contact forces (vertical) [B1]
Forward friction on rear wheel and air resistance (horizontal) [B1]
Each pair balanced – resultant force zero [B1]

questions.prompt: A cyclist of combined mass 30 kg decelerates uniformly to rest over 8.0 m in 5.0 s. Calculate the average resistive force. (4)
A uniform 11.0 m beam of mass 3.0 × 10⁴ kg pivots 6.0 m from one end and is held horizontal by a vertical rod at that end. Calculate the force in the rod. (4)
questions.solution:
Centre of mass is 5.5 m from the rod end, so 0.5 m from the pivot on the rod side [M1]
Moment of weight = 3.0 × 10⁴ × 9.81 × 0.5 = 1.47 × 10⁵ N m [M1]
T × 6.0 = 1.47 × 10⁵ [M1]
T = 2.5 × 10⁴ N [A1]

questions.prompt: A steam engine lifts 3000 kg of water through 10 m every minute, all day. It burns 1500 kg of coal per day; 1 kg of coal releases 22.3 MJ. Deduce whether a claimed efficiency of 10% is correct. (5)
questions.solution:
Useful power = 3000 × 9.81 × 10 ÷ 60 = 4.9 kW [M1]
Useful energy per day = 4.9 × 10³ × 86 400 = 4.2 × 10⁸ J [M1]
Input = 1500 × 22.3 × 10⁶ = 3.3 × 10¹⁰ J [M1]
Efficiency = 1.3% [M1]
Claim is incorrect [A1]

questions.prompt: A water rocket accelerates uniformly from rest to 18 m s⁻¹ in 0.50 s then decelerates at 9.81 m s⁻². Calculate the maximum height reached. (3)
questions.solution:
Powered stage: ½ × 0.50 × 18 = 4.5 m [M1]
Coasting: 18² ÷ (2 × 9.81) = 16.5 m [M1]
Total = 21 m [A1]

questions.prompt: Explain what can be concluded about the forces on an object falling at terminal velocity. (2)
questions.solution:
Resultant force is zero [B1]
Drag (plus upthrust) equals weight [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why the horizontal and vertical motion of a projectile can be treated independently, ignoring air resistance. (2)
questions.solution:
Only force is weight, acting vertically [B1]
Horizontal velocity constant; vertical acceleration g [B1]

questions.prompt: State the base units of impulse. (1)
questions.solution: kg m s⁻¹ [B1]

questions.prompt: A ball leaves a table horizontally and passes through two strips 0.50 m apart horizontally in 0.10 s. Calculate its horizontal speed and how far it has fallen. (3)
A cricket ball is hit at 24 m s⁻¹ at 45° towards a fielder 50 m away. It can only be caught if less than 3 m above its launch height when it reaches him. Deduce whether he can catch it. (5)
A 2000 kg car accelerates from rest to 25 m s⁻¹ in 4.0 s with a motor output of 400 kW. Calculate the work done against resistive forces. (3)
questions.solution:
Energy supplied = 400 × 10³ × 4.0 = 1.6 × 10⁶ J [M1]
Ek = ½ × 2000 × 25² = 6.25 × 10⁵ J [M1]
Work against resistance = 9.8 × 10⁵ J [A1]

questions.prompt: Explain how an airbag reduces injury using the idea of impulse. (2)
questions.solution:
Impulse (change in momentum) is the same [B1]
Spread over a longer time, so force is smaller [B1]

questions.prompt: A boiler receives 25 kW of fuel energy and delivers 21 kW to the water. Calculate its efficiency. (2)

(i) Define the moment of a force. (1)
(ii) An 11.0 m bus (uniform weight 30 000 N) carries gold of weight 30 000 N acting 1.5 m from the back and robbers of weight 9000 N acting 1.0 m from the front. Find where the bus balances, measured from the back. (4)
questions.solution:
(i) Force × perpendicular distance from the line of action to the point [B1]
(ii) Moments: 30 000 × 5.5 + 30 000 × 1.5 + 9000 × 10.0 = 3.0 × 10⁵ N m [M1]
Total weight 69 000 N [M1]
x = 3.0 × 10⁵ ÷ 69 000 [M1]
= 4.3 m from the back [A1]

questions.prompt:
A train accelerates uniformly from rest to 360 km h⁻¹ in 400 s.
(i) Calculate its acceleration. (2)
(ii) Deduce whether it reaches this speed within 25 km. (2)
questions.solution:
(i) v = 100 m s⁻¹ [M1]
a = 0.25 m s⁻² [A1]
(ii) s = ½ × 100 × 400 = 20 km [M1]
Less than 25 km, so yes [A1]

questions.prompt: A 70 kg person is in a lift accelerating upwards at 2.0 m s⁻². Calculate the normal reaction. (2)
A ball is thrown upwards at 15 m s⁻¹ at 40° to the horizontal. Calculate its maximum height. (2)
A 60 kg cyclist climbs 20 m in 50 s with an output power of 300 W. Calculate the work done against resistive forces. (2)
questions.solution:
Energy supplied = 15 000 J; GPE = 11 800 J [M1]
Work against resistance = 3.2 × 10³ J [A1]

questions.prompt:
(i) State why the area under a force-time graph is impulse. (1)
(ii) A 0.046 kg golf ball at rest receives an impulse of 1.4 N s. Calculate its speed. (2)
questions.solution:
(i) Area = FΔt = change in momentum [B1]
(ii) v = 1.4 ÷ 0.046 [M1]
= 30 m s⁻¹ [A1]

questions.prompt: A golf ball is hit at 30 m s⁻¹ at 35° to the horizontal. Calculate its time of flight and range on level ground. (4)

A maglev train reaches 97 m s⁻¹ from rest in 120 s, then covers the rest of a 29.9 km journey in a further 320 s.
(i) Calculate its acceleration. (2)
(ii) Calculate its average speed after the acceleration phase. (2)
questions.solution:
(i) a = 97 ÷ 120 = 0.81 m s⁻² [M1 A1]
(ii) Distance accelerating = ½ × 97 × 120 = 5.8 km [M1]
(29.9 − 5.8) km ÷ 320 s = 75 m s⁻¹ [A1]

questions.prompt: Explain why magnetic levitation is an advantage for high-speed trains. (2)
questions.solution:
No contact between train and track [B1]
Removes rolling friction, allowing higher speeds / less wear [B1]

questions.prompt: State the base units of charge. (1)
questions.solution: A s [B1]

questions.prompt:
A shot is thrown at 14.2 m s⁻¹ at 37.0° to the horizontal and lands 1.98 s later.
(i) Show the vertical component of velocity is about 8.6 m s⁻¹. (2)
(ii) Calculate the launch height. (3)
Calculate the horizontal range of a shot thrown at 14.2 m s⁻¹, 37.0° above the horizontal, with time of flight 1.98 s. (3)
A cyclist accelerates from rest on grass until reaching a constant speed. Explain the shape of the v–t graph. (3)
questions.solution:
Initially large resultant force: steep gradient [B1]
Resistive forces increase with speed, so acceleration falls [B1]
Driving force = resistive forces: constant speed [B1]

questions.prompt: Criticise the claim that all the work done by a cyclist becomes kinetic energy. (2)
questions.solution:
Work is also done against friction / air resistance [B1]
Some energy is transferred thermally to the surroundings [B1]

questions.prompt: A 0.50 kg trolley and a 1.0 kg trolley each move at 2.0 m s⁻¹ towards each other. Find the total momentum. (1)
questions.solution: 1.0 kg m s⁻¹ (in the 1.0 kg trolley's direction) [B1]

questions.prompt: A friction-free trolley released from rest on a 4° ± 1° ramp reaches 1.5 m s⁻¹ after 2.0 s. Determine whether the measured angle is within the stated uncertainty. (4)

(i) State two conditions for equilibrium. (2)
(ii) A 260 g pan hangs 0.18 m from a lever's pivot. Calculate the counterweight needed 0.04 m from the pivot. (2)
questions.solution:
(i) Resultant force is zero [B1]
Resultant moment about any point is zero [B1]
(ii) W × 0.04 = 0.260 × 9.81 × 0.18 [M1]
W = 11 N [A1]

questions.prompt:
(i) Show an 18 kg curling stone at 2.1 m s⁻¹ has momentum of about 40 N s. (1)
(ii) After hitting an identical stationary stone, which moves off at 2.0 m s⁻¹, stone A slides 1.9 m with deceleration 0.10 m s⁻². Deduce whether the collision was elastic. (4)
questions.solution:
(i) p = 18 × 2.1 = 38 N s [B1]
(ii) vA = √(2 × 0.10 × 1.9) = 0.62 m s⁻¹ [M1]
KE before = ½ × 18 × 2.1² = 40 J [M1]
KE after = ½ × 18 × (2.0² + 0.62²) = 39 J [M1]
KE (almost) conserved, so approximately elastic [A1]

questions.prompt: A 75 kg cyclist uses 190 W at 8.3 m s⁻¹ on the flat. Assuming the same resistive force, deduce whether 330 W gives 5.6 m s⁻¹ up a 1-in-20 hill. (4)
questions.solution:
Resistance = 190 ÷ 8.3 = 23 N [M1]
Weight component = 75 × 9.81 ÷ 20 = 37 N [M1]
v = 330 ÷ 60 [M1]
= 5.5 m s⁻¹ – consistent with 5.6 m s⁻¹ [A1]

questions.prompt: A children's book says lift and gravity on a plane are a Newton's third law pair, and that equal forces mean the plane is at rest. Criticise this. (3)
questions.solution:
Third law pairs act on different bodies and are the same type of force [B1]
Lift and weight both act on the plane, so they aren't a pair [B1]
Balanced forces mean constant velocity, not necessarily rest [B1]

questions.prompt:
(i) A cylinder's light-gate times are 7.85, 7.81, 7.79 and 7.80 ms. Is omitting 7.85 ms justified? (1)
(ii) Calculate its velocity after falling 0.75 m from rest. (2)
questions.solution:
(i) Yes – it's well outside the spread of the others [B1]
(ii) v = √(2 × 9.81 × 0.75) [M1]
= 3.8 m s⁻¹ [A1]

questions.prompt:
Two resistors, 100 $\Omega$ and 200 $\Omega$, are connected in series to an ideal 6 V supply.
(a) Calculate the current. (2)
(b) Calculate the potential difference across the 200 $\Omega$ resistor. (2)
(c) Explain how the total current would change if the resistors were connected in parallel instead. (2)
questions.solution:
(a) $R_T=300\,\Omega$, so $I=V/R=0.0200$ A. [M1 A1]
(b) $V_2=IR_2=4.00$ V. [M1 A1]
(c) Parallel connection gives a smaller total resistance than either branch, so for the same supply voltage the total current is larger. [B1 B1]

questions.prompt: A motor's wiring dissipates 60 W when the current is 20 A. Calculate its resistance. (2)
A potentiometer track is 100 mm long and 4.0 mm wide, with resistance 10.0 kΩ. The material's resistivity is 0.50 Ω m. Calculate the track thickness. (3)

A 12 V battery of internal resistance 2.0 Ω supplies a 10 kΩ potentiometer in series with a resistor R. The output across the potentiometer is 10 V. Calculate R and explain why the battery's internal resistance has little effect. (3)
questions.solution:
I = 10 ÷ 10 000 = 1.0 mA [M1]
R = 2.0 ÷ 1.0 × 10⁻³ = 2.0 kΩ [A1]
r is tiny compared with the circuit resistance so lost volts are negligible [B1]

questions.prompt: Calculate the resistance of 1.00 m of nichrome wire of diameter 0.40 mm (ρ = 1.10 × 10⁻⁶ Ω m). (3)

A 1.50 V cell is connected across a uniform 1.00 m wire.
(i) Describe how potential varies along the wire. (1)
(ii) Calculate the p.d. between one end and a point 60.0 cm along. (2)
questions.solution:
(i) Increases uniformly / linearly with distance [B1]
(ii) 1.50 × 0.600 [M1]
= 0.90 V [A1]

questions.prompt: Explain the effect of increased internal resistance on the current and terminal p.d. of a circuit. (2)
questions.solution:
Current decreases [B1]
Terminal p.d. decreases (more lost volts per amp) [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain, in terms of charge carriers, why the current through an LDR increases with light intensity. (2)
questions.solution:
Light releases more charge carriers [B1]
Resistance falls so current increases [B1]

questions.prompt:
A lamp in series with a 500 Ω resistor and a 12 V supply carries 18 mA.
(i) Calculate the p.d. across the lamp. (2)
(ii) Explain why connecting a 1.5 kΩ voltmeter across the lamp reduces its p.d. (1)
questions.solution:
(i) V_R = 0.018 × 500 = 9.0 V [M1]
Lamp p.d. = 3.0 V [A1]
(ii) Voltmeter in parallel lowers the combined resistance, so it takes a smaller share of the p.d. [B1]

questions.prompt: Compare a potential divider circuit and a variable resistor circuit for obtaining a full I–V characteristic of a lamp. (3)
questions.solution:
Potential divider can vary p.d. from 0 V up to the supply [B1]
Variable resistor can't reduce p.d. to zero [B1]
Potential divider gives the full range of data, so it is more suitable [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain, in terms of charge carriers, why the p.d. across a fixed resistor in series with an NTC thermistor falls as the water cools. (3)
questions.solution:
As temperature falls, fewer charge carriers are released in the thermistor [B1]
Thermistor resistance increases [B1]
It takes a larger share of the p.d., so the fixed resistor's p.d. falls [B1]

questions.prompt: A constant current flows through a wire whose cross-section gets smaller. Explain the effect on drift velocity. (2)
questions.solution:
Same current and number density [B1]
Smaller A, so drift velocity increases [B1]

questions.prompt: Show that the units of ρ = E/j match, where E is electric field strength and j = I/A is current density. (3)
questions.solution:
E in V m⁻¹, j in A m⁻² [M1]
E/j in V m A⁻¹ [M1]
= Ω m, the unit of resistivity [A1]

questions.prompt: An LDR is in series with a 300 Ω resistor across 6.0 V. A transistor connected across the LDR switches on when its p.d. exceeds 0.70 V. Calculate the LDR resistance at switching and state whether this happens as the light gets brighter or darker. (4)
hints: LDR R rises in the dark.
questions.solution:
0.70 = 6.0R ÷ (R + 300) [M1]
R = 0.70 × 300 ÷ 5.30 [M1]
= 40 Ω [A1]
Switches on as it gets darker (R rises above 40 Ω) [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why an increase in a car battery's internal resistance is a disadvantage. (2)
questions.solution:
More lost volts, so less terminal p.d. / power to the motor [B1]
More energy wasted heating the battery [B1]

questions.prompt: A 700 km copper cable of diameter 15 cm (ρ = 1.7 × 10⁻⁸ Ω m) transmits 1400 MW at 1000 kV. Deduce whether the transmission is nearly 100% efficient. (6)
Show that a bulb rated 2.5 V, 0.50 W has an operating resistance of 12.5 Ω. (2)
A 1.0 F uncharged capacitor is connected in series with a 12.5 Ω bulb and a 2.5 V supply. Describe and explain how the bulb's brightness changes. (3)
questions.solution:
Initially full current, bulb at full brightness [B1]
Current falls exponentially as the capacitor charges [B1]
Bulb dims over about RC = 12.5 s and goes out [B1]

questions.prompt: State which quantity is constant along a wire whose cross-section varies, and which changes. (2)
questions.solution:
Current is constant [B1]
Drift velocity changes (larger where thinner) [B1]

questions.prompt: A solar panel has emf 8.0 V and terminal p.d. 5.6 V when supplying 0.40 A. Calculate its internal resistance. (3)
400 panels each deliver 0.40 A at 5.6 V to charge a 12 kWh battery. Calculate the charging time. (3)
A meter of resistance 600 Ω reads full scale at 2.0 mA. Calculate the series resistor needed to read up to 10 V. (3)
A 12 V battery with internal resistance 0.50 Ω lights a bulb rated 40 W at 12 V. Calculate the terminal p.d. (4)
A second identical bulb is switched on in parallel. Explain the effect on the first bulb's brightness. (3)
questions.solution:
Total resistance falls, current from battery increases [B1]
More lost volts across internal resistance [B1]
Terminal p.d. falls, first bulb dims [B1]

questions.prompt: A student says a straight-line I–V graph for a lamp between 3 V and 12 V shows it obeys Ohm's law. Evaluate this. (3)
questions.solution:
Ohm's law requires I ∝ V – line through the origin [B1]
Data don't extend below 2.5 V [B1]
Gradient changes / doesn't pass through origin, so claim invalid [B1]

questions.prompt: Derive 1/R = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂ for two resistors in parallel. (3)
questions.solution:
Same p.d. V across each [B1]
I = I₁ + I₂ [B1]
V/R = V/R₁ + V/R₂, giving 1/R = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂ [B1]

questions.prompt: Electrodes 28 mm × 0.50 mm are 0.60 mm apart in salt water (ρ = 1.6 Ω m) with a 1.5 V cell. Show the current is about 20 mA. (3)
Define the volt. (1)
questions.solution: One joule per coulomb [B1]

questions.prompt: An LDR and fixed resistor in series across 6 V each have 3.0 V in daylight. Describe the change in p.d. across the LDR in darkness. (2)
questions.solution:
LDR resistance increases [B1]
p.d. across it rises towards 6 V [B1]

questions.prompt: A 2600 W iron's 890 g steel plate (c = 450 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹) heats from 18 °C to 215 °C. Deduce whether this takes under a minute. (3)

(i) Describe the I–V graph of a diode. (1)
(ii) Calculate the protective resistor for an LED rated 20 mA, 3.2 V on 5.0 V. (2)
questions.solution:
(i) No current in reverse; current rises steeply above a threshold forward p.d. [B1]
(ii) R = (5.0 − 3.2) ÷ 0.020 [M1]
= 90 Ω [A1]

questions.prompt: A 104 cm² solar cell gives a maximum of 2.0 W in 1000 W m⁻² sunlight. Calculate its efficiency. (2)
A wire's diameter is doubled at the same length. State its new resistance. (1)

(i) Show an 8.5 V rms supply across 1.5 Ω gives about 48 W. (1)
(ii) Calculate the time to heat 1.25 × 10⁻⁴ m³ of milk by 12 °C (c = 3930 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹, ρ = 1050 kg m⁻³). (3)
An LED with 1.9 V across it takes 18 mA from a 5.0 V supply through a resistor. Calculate the resistance. (2)
Nichrome wire is 0.27 ± 0.01 mm in diameter and 1.25 ± 0.05 m long. Which measurement contributes most to the uncertainty in resistivity? (2)
questions.solution:
Diameter: 2 × 3.7% = 7.4%; length 4% [M1]
Diameter contributes most [A1]

questions.prompt:
A wire of original length 1.2 m and cross-sectional area 1.5 × 10⁻⁶ m$^2$ extends by 0.8 mm under a tensile force of 120 N.
(a) Calculate the stress. (2)
(b) Calculate the strain. (2)
(c) Hence calculate Young modulus. (2)
questions.solution:
(a) Stress $=F/A=8.000\times10^{7}$ Pa. [M1 A1]
(b) Strain $=\Delta L/L=6.667\times10^{-4}$. [M1 A1]
(c) $E=\text{stress}/\text{strain}=1.200\times10^{11}$ Pa. [M1 A1]

questions.prompt: An 80 kg dummy at 25 m s⁻¹ is stopped by a seat belt of cross-section 0.90 cm² and length 2.0 m. Show that the belt must absorb about 1.4 × 10⁸ J m⁻³. (3)
questions.solution:
Ek = ½ × 80 × 25² = 2.5 × 10⁴ J [M1]
Volume = 0.90 × 10⁻⁴ × 2.0 = 1.8 × 10⁻⁴ m³ [M1]
Energy per unit volume = 1.4 × 10⁸ J m⁻³ [A1]

questions.prompt: Show that the area under a stress-strain graph gives the energy stored per unit volume. (2)
questions.solution:
Area = stress × strain = (F/A)(x/L) [M1]
= ½Fx ÷ AL = energy ÷ volume [A1]

questions.prompt:
(i) Show that the terminal velocity of a small sphere (ignoring upthrust) is v = 2ρgr²/9η. (2)
(ii) State one condition for Stokes' law to apply. (1)
questions.solution:
(i) (4/3)πr³ρg = 6πηrv [M1]
Rearranges to v = 2ρgr²/9η [A1]
(ii) Laminar flow / small spherical object / low speed [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why Stokes' law overestimates the terminal velocity of large raindrops. (2)
questions.solution:
At high speeds flow becomes turbulent [B1]
Drag is much greater than Stokes' law predicts / drops deform [B1]

questions.prompt:
A ball bearing of radius 5.0 mm (density 7750 kg m⁻³) falls 25.0 cm through honey (density 1360 kg m⁻³) in a mean time of 6.37 s.
(i) Calculate its terminal velocity. (1)
(ii) Calculate the viscosity using η = 2r²g(ρ_B − ρ_H)/9v. (3)
Criticise timing the ball between rubber bands by eye and suggest an improvement. (2)
questions.solution:
Parallax and reaction time errors / ball may not have reached terminal velocity at the first band [B1]
Use video with a scale / light gates; place first band well below surface [B1]

9 maxima [B1]

⁸⁷₃₇Rb → ⁸⁷₃₈Sr + ⁰₋₁e [M1]
+ ν̄ₑ [A1]

questions.prompt: A sample of radium-226 (half-life 1600 years) has activity 2.0 Bq. Calculate the number of radium nuclei. (3)
²²⁶Ra (225.97713 u) decays to ²²²Rn (221.97040 u) and an alpha particle (4.00151 u). Calculate the energy released in MeV. (3)
Explain why a GM tube outside a sealed bottle detects beta but not alpha radiation from protactinium. (2)
questions.solution:
Alpha is absorbed by the solvent and plastic [B1]
Beta penetrates the bottle wall [B1]

questions.prompt: A caesium-137 source (half-life 30 years) has activity 1.0 × 10¹⁶ Bq. Calculate the time for its activity to fall to 100 Bq. (4)
Protactinium-231 (Z = 91) emits an alpha particle. Give the daughter nucleus. (1)
questions.solution: ²²⁷₈₉Ac [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why repeated background counts from a GM tube vary. (2)
questions.solution:
Radioactive decay is random [B1]
Count over a long time and average [B1]

questions.prompt: A nuclear reaction has a mass decrease of 0.05 u. Calculate the energy released in MeV. (2)

(i) Explain the meaning of spontaneous and random in radioactive decay. (2)
(ii) Explain why a decay constant can be found despite decay being random. (2)
questions.solution:
(i) Spontaneous: not affected by external factors [B1]
Random: can't predict which nucleus will decay or when [B1]
(ii) Each nucleus has a constant probability of decay [B1]
With very large numbers, the decay rate is predictable [B1]

questions.prompt: Calculate the percentage of americium-241 (half-life 432 years) remaining after 40 years. (3)
Describe how to use a GM tube to find the percentage of a source's activity due to beta radiation. (4)
questions.solution:
Measure background count, then count with the source [B1]
Insert paper to remove alpha; record count [B1]
Insert aluminium (few mm) to remove beta; record count [B1]
Difference between paper and aluminium counts ÷ total corrected count gives beta % [B1]

questions.prompt: 5.5 keV electrons are diffracted by gold foil. State what this shows about electrons. (2)
questions.solution:
Electrons behave as waves [B1]
Wavelength comparable to atomic spacing (λ = h/p) [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how high-frequency radiation is produced when fast electrons hit metal atoms. (4)
questions.solution:
Fast electrons knock out inner-shell electrons [B1]
Outer electrons drop into the vacancies [B1]
Energy gaps are large [B1]
So high-energy (X-ray) photons are emitted, hf = ΔE [B1]

questions.prompt: State which photoelectric observation could also be explained by the wave model. (1)
questions.solution: Emission rate increasing with intensity [B1]

questions.prompt: Complete the decay equation for potassium-40 (Z = 19) decaying by β⁻ to calcium. (2)
questions.solution:
⁴⁰₁₉K → ⁴⁰₂₀Ca + ⁰₋₁e [B1]
+ ν̄ₑ [B1]

questions.prompt: A 300 mg sample contains 8.1 × 10²¹ potassium nuclei per gram, 0.012% of them K-40. Show there are about 3 × 10¹⁷ K-40 nuclei. (2)
Show 2.9 × 10¹⁷ K-40 nuclei (half-life 1.25 × 10⁹ years) have activity about 5 Bq. (3)
Background is 15 counts min⁻¹. With a 5.1 Bq source, 176 counts are recorded in 10 minutes. Decide whether the GM tube detects at least 7.5% of the betas. (3)
questions.solution:
Corrected = 176 − 150 = 26 counts in 600 s [M1]
Efficiency = 0.043 ÷ 5.1 = 0.85% [M1]
Below 7.5%, so not efficient [A1]

questions.prompt: Explain why a GM tube detects only a small fraction of a source's decays. (2)
questions.solution:
Radiation is emitted in all directions; few enter the tube [B1]
Some betas are absorbed by the sample / air / tube window [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why K-40 (half-life 1.25 × 10⁹ years) is a better test source than Sr-90 (29 years). (1)
questions.solution: Activity effectively constant over the source's lifetime [B1]

questions.prompt:
Cs-137 (half-life 9.5 × 10⁸ s) gives 2.5 × 10⁴ Bq per kg of a sample.
(i) Complete its β⁻ decay to barium. (2)
(ii) Calculate the Cs-137 atoms per kg. (2)
(iii) Calculate the time for 10% to decay. (2)
questions.solution:
(i) ¹³⁷₅₅Cs → ¹³⁷₅₆Ba + ⁰₋₁e [B1]
+ ν̄ₑ [B1]
(ii) λ = 7.3 × 10⁻¹⁰ s⁻¹ [M1]
N = 3.4 × 10¹³ [A1]
(iii) t = ln(1/0.90) ÷ 7.3 × 10⁻¹⁰ [M1]
= 1.4 × 10⁸ s [A1]

questions.prompt:
(i) Complete the alpha decay of radon-220. (1)
(ii) Test the claim that activity falls below 1% within 450 s (half-life 55.6 s). (2)
questions.solution:
(i) ²²⁰₈₆Rn → ²¹⁶₈₄Po + ⁴₂He [B1]
(ii) 450 ÷ 55.6 = 8.1 half-lives [M1]
(½)^8.1 = 0.4%, so correct [A1]

questions.prompt:
(i) Explain what spontaneous decay means. (1)
(ii) Explain why decay rate decreases exponentially for a large sample. (2)
questions.solution:
(i) Not affected by external factors [B1]
(ii) Each nucleus has a constant probability of decay, so rate ∝ N [B1]
As N falls, rate falls in proportion: exponential [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain one modification needed for an inverse square test with radium-226 rather than cobalt-60. (2)
questions.solution:
Radium also emits α and β [B1]
Place an absorber (aluminium) to remove them, so only γ is measured [B1]

questions.prompt:
A spherical body has mass $5.97\times10^{24}$ kg and radius $6.37\times10^{6}$ m.
(a) Calculate the gravitational field strength at its surface. Use $G=6.67\times10^{-11}$ N m$^2$ kg$^{-2}$. (3)
(b) State how field strength changes with distance outside the body. (2)
(c) Explain why gravitational potential is negative when zero is defined at infinity. (2)
hints: Potential is defined relative to infinity.
questions.solution:
(a) $g=GM/r^2=9.81$ N kg$^{-1}$. [M1 M1 A1]
(b) Outside a spherical body $g\propto1/r^2$. [B1 B1]
(c) Work must be supplied to move a mass from the field to infinity, so bound positions have lower (negative) potential relative to the zero at infinity. [B1 B1]

questions.prompt: A 1000 kg spacecraft descends from 10.0 km to 2.0 km above Mars (M = 6.4 × 10²³ kg, R = 3390 km). Calculate the change in gravitational potential energy. (3)
A probe orbits Mercury (M = 3.30 × 10²³ kg, R = 2440 km) 7000 km above the surface. Calculate the orbital period in hours. (4)
An object is released from rest 15 000 km above Mercury's surface. Calculate its speed on reaching the surface. (4)
Explain one advantage of a highly elliptical orbit for a probe studying a hot planet. (2)
questions.solution:
Spends much of each orbit far from the planet [B1]
Allows the probe to cool / avoid excessive heating [B1]

questions.prompt: The Hubble Space Telescope orbits at 7.60 km s⁻¹. Show that its height is about 5 × 10⁵ m (M_E = 5.97 × 10²⁴ kg, R_E = 6.37 × 10⁶ m). (3)
Explain why giving a satellite extra energy raises its orbit but reduces its orbital speed. (3)
questions.solution:
Extra energy increases gravitational potential energy so radius increases [B1]
Orbital speed v = √(GM/r) decreases with r [B1]
Kinetic energy decreases while total energy increases [B1]

questions.prompt: Europa orbits Jupiter at a radius of 6.71 × 10⁸ m with a period of 85.2 hours. Calculate Jupiter's mass. (4)
A planet has half Earth's diameter and one ninth of its mass. Calculate its surface gravity. (2)
State how field strength and potential vary with distance from a point mass. (2)
questions.solution:
Field strength ∝ 1/r² [B1]
Potential ∝ −1/r [B1]

questions.prompt: Calculate the orbital speed of the ISS at radius 6800 km (M_E = 6.0 × 10²⁴ kg). (3)
Explain why astronauts on the ISS have zero apparent weight. (2)
questions.solution:
They and the ISS accelerate towards Earth at the same rate [B1]
No normal contact force acts [B1]

questions.prompt: An astronaut on a 6.0 kg platform attached to a spring (k = 400 N m⁻¹) oscillates at 0.35 Hz. Calculate the astronaut's mass. (4)
questions.solution:
m_total = k ÷ (4π²f²) [M1]
= 400 ÷ (4π² × 0.35²) [M1]
= 83 kg [M1]
Astronaut = 77 kg [A1]

questions.prompt: Give one similarity and one difference between gravitational and electric fields. (2)
questions.solution:
Both follow inverse square laws for point sources [B1]
Gravity is only attractive / acts on all masses; electric acts only on charges [B1]

questions.prompt:
Bennu has radius 245 m and density 1260 kg m⁻³ and is 7.49 × 10⁸ m from Earth (5.98 × 10²⁴ kg).
(i) Show its mass is about 7.8 × 10¹⁰ kg. (2)
(ii) Calculate the force between Bennu and Earth. (2)
Bennu orbits the Sun every 1.17 years at 1.70 × 10¹¹ m (1 year = 3.15 × 10⁷ s). Calculate the Sun's mass. (3)
An 80 g toy on a spring extends it by 10.0 cm. Deduce whether a stated oscillation frequency of 2.5 Hz is correct. (5)

(i) Calculate the period of a 1.50 m pendulum. (2)
(ii) Calculate its maximum speed for an amplitude of 8.0 cm. (3)
Explain why the oscillations of a spring toy die away. (2)
questions.solution:
Air resistance / internal friction acts on the toy [B1]
Energy is transferred to the surroundings, so amplitude decreases [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why energy transfers between two coupled pendulums of equal length, but hardly at all if their lengths differ. (4)
questions.solution:
Pendulum A drives B through the coupling [B1]
Equal lengths give equal natural frequencies [B1]
Driving at the natural frequency gives resonance and large energy transfer [B1]
Different lengths: driving frequency ≠ natural frequency, so small response [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe the velocity-time graph of a simple harmonic oscillator whose displacement is x = A sin ωt. (2)
questions.solution:
Cosine curve of amplitude Aω [B1]
Leads displacement by π/2 [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how the maximum kinetic energy of an SHM oscillator changes when its amplitude is doubled. (3)
questions.solution:
Period unchanged so ω unchanged [B1]
v_max doubles [B1]
Max KE quadruples [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how to improve the measurement of a metronome's period, timed for one swing from extreme to extreme. (3)
questions.solution:
Time a full oscillation, not half [B1]
Time many oscillations (e.g. 20) and divide [B1]
Use a fiducial marker at the centre where it moves fastest; repeat and average [B1]

questions.prompt:
Each of a car's four springs is compressed 0.150 m by a quarter of the car's 1200 kg weight.
(i) Show that the stiffness of each spring is about 2.0 × 10⁴ N m⁻¹. (3)
(ii) Calculate the frequency of vertical oscillations. (3)
Explain why high-viscosity oil in a car's shock absorbers gives heavy damping. (3)
questions.solution:
Viscous oil provides a large resistive force on the moving piston [B1]
Energy is removed quickly from the oscillation [B1]
Body returns slowly without oscillating [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how kinetic energy varies with displacement in SHM. (2)
questions.solution:
Kinetic energy is maximum at x = 0 [B1]
Falls to zero at ±A along a parabola [B1]

questions.prompt: The mass above (83 kg) oscillates at 0.35 Hz with peak-to-peak displacement 0.30 m. Calculate its maximum acceleration. (3)

A trolley of mass 0.90 kg between springs resonates at 2.0 Hz.
(i) Explain the shape of the amplitude-frequency graph. (2)
(ii) Calculate the effective spring constant. (2)
questions.solution:
(i) Amplitude peaks when driving frequency equals natural frequency [B1]
Damping limits the peak height [B1]
(ii) k = 4π² × 2.0² × 0.90 [M1]
= 140 N m⁻¹ [A1]

questions.prompt: A trolley in SHM has amplitude 6.0 cm and period 0.50 s. Calculate its maximum velocity. (2)
questions.solution:
ω = 12.6 rad s⁻¹ [M1]
v = 0.75 m s⁻¹ [A1]

questions.prompt:
(i) Calculate the length of a pendulum with period 2.40 s. (2)
(ii) Explain why a pendulum with a paper cone loses amplitude. (2)
questions.solution:
(i) l = 9.81 × 2.40² ÷ 4π² [M1]
= 1.43 m [A1]
(ii) Large air resistance on the cone [B1]
Energy transferred to the surroundings each swing [B1]

questions.prompt: Amplitude follows A = A₀e^(−kt). Explain how a graph of ln A against t gives A₀ and k. (3)
questions.solution:
ln A = ln A₀ − kt [B1]
Gradient = −k [B1]
Intercept = ln A₀ [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe the velocity-time graph corresponding to an acceleration-time graph a = −a₀ sin ωt. (2)
questions.solution:
Velocity is a cosine curve [B1]
Leads displacement by π/2; maximum when acceleration is zero [B1]

questions.prompt: State what is meant by simple harmonic motion. (2)
questions.solution:
Acceleration proportional to displacement [B1]
Always directed towards the equilibrium position [B1]

questions.prompt: The amplitude of an oscillator doubles at the same frequency. Explain how its maximum kinetic energy changes. (2)
questions.solution:
Maximum speed doubles [B1]
Maximum kinetic energy quadruples [B1]

questions.prompt: A swing completes 24 oscillations in one minute. Calculate its frequency. (1)
A tower sways with amplitude 0.90 m at its natural frequency of 0.17 Hz. Calculate its maximum velocity. (2)
Two springs (k = 22 N m⁻¹ each) in series hold a 120 g magnet. Calculate the oscillation frequency. (3)
A pendulum takes 1.00 s to swing from one side to the other. Calculate its length. (2)
Explain how the resonant driving frequency changes for a heavier baby in a bouncer. (3)
questions.solution:
Natural frequency ∝ √(k/m) [B1]
Larger mass gives lower natural frequency [B1]
Resonance (maximum amplitude) occurs at a lower driving frequency [B1]

questions.prompt:
A student plots a graph to test a proposed linear relationship between two physical quantities.
(a) Explain how the gradient can be used to determine a physical constant. (2)
(b) Describe two ways to reduce uncertainty in the gradient. (2)
(c) Explain why a straight-line graph alone does not prove the proposed model is exact. (2)
hints: A large gradient triangle reduces percentage reading uncertainty.
questions.solution:
(a) Rearrange the model into $y=mx+c$ and identify the constant from the theoretical expression for $m$. [M1 A1]
(b) Use a wide range of values and a best-fit line/large triangle; repeat measurements where appropriate. [B1 B1]
(c) Experimental uncertainty and a limited data range may hide small systematic deviations from the model. [B1 B1]

questions.prompt:
Wind speed v and Beaufort number B follow v = kBᵖ. B = 1 gives v = 2.00 m s⁻¹ and B = 9 gives 50.5 m s⁻¹.
(i) Explain why log v against log B is a straight line. (2)
(ii) Determine p and k. (2)
hints: log v = p log B + log k.
questions.solution:
(i) log v = p log B + log k [M1]
Form y = mx + c [A1]
(ii) p = log(50.5/2.00) ÷ log 9 = 1.47 [B1]
k = 2.00 (from B = 1) [B1]

questions.prompt: V = V₀e^(−bθ). Explain how to determine b and V₀ from a graph. (4)
questions.solution:
Plot ln V against θ [B1]
ln V = ln V₀ − bθ is a straight line [B1]
Gradient = −b [B1]
Intercept = ln V₀ so V₀ = e^(intercept) [B1]

questions.prompt: Two microphones on an oscilloscope come back into phase after one is moved 20.5 cm. The trace shows a period of 3 divisions at 0.20 ms per division. Calculate the speed of sound. (4)
Suggest how to improve the measurement of wavelength using two microphones. (2)
questions.solution:
Move through several wavelengths and divide [B1]
Reduces percentage uncertainty [B1]

questions.prompt: A student records trapped-air lengths at four temperatures only, with a thermometer of resolution 0.5 °C. Criticise the results. (3)
questions.solution:
Too few readings to establish a trend [B1]
Uneven spacing / limited range [B1]
Inconsistent precision / no repeats [B1]

questions.prompt: Two clay spheres of the same material have diameters 2.0 cm and 4.0 cm and are dropped from the same height. Find the factor by which the kinetic energy at impact increases. (3)
questions.solution:
Same drop height so same impact speed [B1]
Mass increases by 2³ = 8 [M1]
KE increases by a factor of 8 [A1]

questions.prompt: Infrared of intensity 2.0 W m⁻² passes through 1.5 mm of blood with μ = 0.50 mm⁻¹. Calculate the transmitted intensity. (3)
Calculate the peak wavelength of a 3000 K halogen lamp and state the region. (2)
A 1.80 × 10⁻⁶ m oil drop (ρ = 900 kg m⁻³) is held between plates 1.50 cm apart at 5000 V. Deduce whether its charge is a whole number of e. (5)
Explain why the student waits before timing an oil drop's fall. (2)
questions.solution:
The drop must first reach terminal velocity [B1]
So the speed measured is constant [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe improvements to measuring the period of a trolley oscillating between springs. (4)
questions.solution:
Time 10 or more oscillations [B1]
Use a fiducial marker at the equilibrium position [B1]
Repeat and calculate a mean [B1]
Or use a light gate / motion sensor and data logger [B1]

questions.prompt: Newton's ring diameters D follow D = pN^q. Explain how to find p and q and predict q. (4)
questions.solution:
Plot log D against log N [B1]
Gradient = q [B1]
Intercept = log p [B1]
Expect q ≈ 0.5 [B1]

questions.prompt: Give one reason a data logger suits monitoring a cell's terminal p.d. as it runs down. (1)
questions.solution: Records readings automatically over a long time [B1]

questions.prompt: Assess whether a data logger would improve the accuracy of a capacitor discharge experiment. (2)
questions.solution:
More frequent readings, no reaction-time error [B1]
But component tolerance / systematic errors aren't removed [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain where an ammeter must be placed to measure a heater's current. (2)
questions.solution:
In series with the heater [B1]
So it measures only the heater current [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe a circuit giving a full range of p.d.s from 0 to 12 V across a lamp. (2)
questions.solution:
Use a potentiometer connected as a potential divider across the supply [B1]
Lamp connected between the slider and one end [B1]

questions.prompt: A loop on a moving trolley touches a resistance wire across a 1.5 V cell. Explain how the recorded p.d. measures position. (3)
questions.solution:
Wire acts as a potential divider [B1]
p.d. between end and contact ∝ length [B1]
So p.d. increases linearly with distance moved [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how to test whether a charge-time graph shows exponential decay. (3)
questions.solution:
Read charge at equal time intervals [B1]
Check the ratio of successive values is constant [B1]
Or plot ln Q against t – a straight line [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why protons may treat deep tumours better than X-rays. (2)
questions.solution:
Protons deposit most energy at a specific depth (Bragg peak) [B1]
Less damage to surrounding healthy tissue [B1]

questions.prompt: A disc has mass 42.5 ± 0.5 g, diameter 5.2 ± 0.1 cm and thickness 1.9 ± 0.1 mm. Calculate its density and percentage uncertainty. (4)

(i) Explain why log η against log T is straight for η = AT^B. (2)
(ii) η is 4.60 mPa s at 123 K and 12.0 mPa s at 473 K. Estimate B. (2)
hints: log η = log A + B log T.
questions.solution:
(i) log η = log A + B log T [B1]
Straight line with gradient B, intercept log A [B1]
(ii) B = log(12.0/4.60) ÷ log(473/123) [M1]
= 0.71 [A1]

questions.prompt: Light-gate times are 7.81, 7.79 and 7.80 ms. Calculate the percentage uncertainty in the mean. (2)
A coin is 1.54 mm thick, 22.16 mm in diameter and 11.2 g in mass. Pure gold is 1.93 × 10⁴ kg m⁻³. Assess whether it's pure gold. (4)
questions.solution:
V = π × (11.08 × 10⁻³)² × 1.54 × 10⁻³ = 5.94 × 10⁻⁷ m³ [M1]
ρ = 1.89 × 10⁴ kg m⁻³ [M1]
2.3% below pure gold; uncertainty about 1.6% (mostly t and m) [M1]
So probably not pure [A1]

questions.prompt: T is 1480 K at 5.03 V and 2280 K at 15.06 V. For T = aV^b, estimate b. (2)
A ball has diameter 5.06 cm (± 0.01 cm) and mass 175 g (± 1 g). Quartz is 2650 kg m⁻³ and glass 2590 kg m⁻³. Deduce what it's made of. (4)
questions.solution:
V = 67.8 cm³; ρ = 2580 kg m⁻³ [M1]
% uncertainty = 3 × 0.2% + 0.6% = 1.2% [M1]
Range 2550–2610 kg m⁻³ [M1]
Includes glass, not quartz [A1]

questions.prompt:
(i) Capillary rise is read as 12.00 cm and 27.10 cm (± 0.05 cm each). Calculate the percentage uncertainty in h. (2)
(ii) r = 0.09 mm gives 16.56 cm and r = 0.15 mm gives 10.33 cm. Test h = k/r. (2)
questions.solution:
(i) h = 15.10 ± 0.10 cm [M1]
0.66% [A1]
(ii) hr = 1.49 and 1.55 [M1]
Differ by 4%, larger than measurement uncertainty, so not exactly k/r [A1]

questions.prompt: Comment on using a light gate instead of a stopwatch when both have 0.01 s resolution. (2)
questions.solution:
Light gate removes human reaction time error [B1]
So more accurate even with the same resolution [B1]
